Today to Thursday: the Inland NW will be in a brief col between 
low pressure to the south and a system off the coast today, before
the offshore system moves in tonight into Thursday morning. 
Through this morning middle to higher clouds will continue to thin
and this will enable some low clouds and patchy fog in the 
sheltered valleys and possibly the Columbia Basin to Palouse and 
L-C Valley; confidence is slower in these latter areas because 
higher clouds could be slower to erode. Later in the afternoon 
into tonight the higher clouds start to increase from the west as 
the system approaches. Rain and mountain snow chances will start 
into the Cascades by late afternoon to early evening. Rain chances
expand to central Washington from late evening to overnight, 
impinging on the eastern third of WA late. By early Thursday 
morning rain chances peak over the east third of WA and ID, before
the best chances shift into Idaho in the late morning and 
afternoon dissipate into Thursday evening. 

This will be mainly mountain snow and valley rain; though some 
rain/snow mix is possible in the northern valleys, especially 
closer to the Canadian border. Precipitation amounts will be 
light, with rain amounts generally less than 0.05 inches and snow 
amounts generally less than 0.5 inches and those will be in the 
higher mountains. Some gusty winds are possible around south-
central to east-central WA and lower ID Thursday afternoon in the 
wake of passing front, with gusts of 15-20 mph. Highs will largely
in the upper 40s to lower 50s today and the upper 40s to upper 
50s Thursday, with milder readings toward the deeper basin and 
cooler readings to the northeast CWA under the clouds and 
precipitation chances. Lows will largely be in the 30s, with some 
upper 20s in the sheltered northern valleys.

Friday to Tuesday: The Inland NW transitions to a more 
progressive westerly flow, with several embedded system tracking 
over the area every other day or so. However westerly flow and 
transient nature of these systems suggest limited precipitation 
potential. The next precipitation chances expand into the Cascades
early Friday and expand toward northeast WA/north ID late Friday 
afternoon through evening. Snow levels start near 3.5-5kft, lowest
in the Cascades and northern mountains, before rising to around 
5-8kft by late afternoon. So some mountain snow accumulations are 
expected around the Cascades, around 0.5 to 1 inch locally higher 
in the higher peaks. Better chances will be early in the day. 
Clouds will be more abundant than precipitation elsewhere then. 

The next more robust system coming on a 110-120Kt jet stream 
arrives Saturday night and Sunday. Precipitation chance rises 
over the Cascades first Saturday night, then expand east through 
the day Sunday. Probabilities still remain best in the Cascades 
and eastern mountains and are held to around 15-25 percent over 
the Upper Columbia Basin, Spokane/C'dA area, Palouse and lower 
ID. Still another system is forecast to come in later Monday into 
Tuesday. All of these have some degree of uncertainty in timing 
given the more progressive/quicker westerly flow as models can 
tend to have trouble with timing in such a flow pattern. 

Snow levels Saturday night start near 6.5-8.5kft, drop to around 
5-7kft by late Sunday morning, then 3-6kft by late Sunday night 
into Monday morning, before moderating back to 6-7kft by Tuesday 
afternoon. So this will mean occasional mountain snow, especially 
the Cascades. These are mainly above pass level, except Washington
Pass. Saturday night into Sunday models show 2-4 inches in the 
mountains; higher peaks could see more. NBM guidance shows about a
30% chance of measurable snow at Stevens Pass and about 80% at 
Washington Pass; but for 1 inch probabilities are 10-15% at 
Stevens and 55% at Washington Pass. Monday night and Tuesday may 
see mountain snow around 0.5-2 inches. The NBM probabilities of 
measurable snow by this time are around 5% at Stevens and 45% at 
Washington Pass 

The other notable feature heading toward Sunday is winds. The
strong jet crossing the area, tightening gradient and increased
mixing shows wind gusts of 20-30 mph Sunday afternoon over the
Waterville Plateau to Upper Columbia Basin east toward the WA/ID
border, as well as the Okanogan valley to Okanogan Highlands.
Strongest winds are forecast for the northeast Waterville Plateau
to Upper Columbia Basin. Highs will be in the upper 40s to mid-50s
much of the period, with slight peak to the mid-50s to lower 60s
Saturday. Lows largely in the 30s are forecast, with some 20s in
the sheltered valleys; Saturday night/Sunday AM will be the
exception with mainly 30s to lower 40s. /Solveig
